title: Crows Decide Twice as Fast as Humans
summary:
Crows are even smarter, and faster, than we thought. New research from the University of Tubingen in Germany found that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, and stay remarkably accurate while doing it.

In the experiments, two carrion crows watched patterns of moving dots on a touchscreen. They had to work out whether most of the dots were moving left or right, then peck a target on the matching side of the screen. On average, the birds needed just 235 milliseconds to decide, less than a quarter of a second. Even when the direction was hard to tell, their choices were still better than random guessing, and with clear signals they were accurate nearly 100 percent of the time.

The researchers, Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder, also recorded the activity of single brain cells as the birds worked. The signals came from a part of the crow brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale, which helps process information and make decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

Just 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared, the brain cells linked to each choice were already showing different patterns of activity, well before the birds pecked their answer. As the crows weighed the evidence, the activity steadily grew until it hit the level linked to making a decision.

The most striking part is that crows seem to use decision-making processes similar to those in humans and other primates, even though bird brains are built very differently: unlike mammals, birds have no layered cerebral cortex. The researchers suggest the speed may come from the demands of a bird's life, since birds rely on vision for fast, precise moves in flight and for guiding their beaks when foraging. Exactly how their differently built brains manage to decide so much faster is still unknown, and more studies will be needed. The findings were published in the journal Science.
why_it_matters: The study shows that very different brains can solve the same problem in similar ways, which could change how scientists think about intelligence and decision-making.

keywords.explanation: Carrion crows are a kind of black crow that often eats dead animals and other food it finds.
A millisecond is one thousandth of a second, a very tiny amount of time.
The nidopallium caudolaterale is a part of a bird's brain that helps it process information and make decisions.
The prefrontal cortex is a part of the human brain that helps with thinking and making decisions.
The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of a mammal's brain, where much thinking happens.
Foraging means searching for food in nature.
